title: Bearing Degradation and Failure
content:
FAULT: Bearing Degradation and Failure
COMPONENT: Rolling element bearings — motors, pumps, fans, gearboxes

SYMPTOMS:
- High vibration levels (typically >7.1 mm/s RMS), often with metallic grinding, squealing, or rumbling noise
- Elevated bearing temperature (>75°C) due to increased friction
- Noise level spikes above 85 dB at the bearing housing
- Irregular vibration signature — may exhibit impacting at fault frequencies (BPFO, BPFI, BSF, FTF)
- Visible pitting, spalling, flaking, or discolouration on bearing races or rolling elements

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): >7.1 warn, >11.0 danger — particularly high in radial direction
- Temperature (°C): bearing housing >75°C warn, >90°C danger
- Noise (dB): >85 dB sustained at machine casing
- RPM: may fluctuate slightly if bearing is severely damaged
- Current (A): marginal increase due to added friction load

ROOT CAUSES:
- Inadequate or contaminated lubrication (most common cause, ~40% of failures)
- Overloading — radial or axial loads exceeding bearing rating
- Misalignment of shaft causing uneven load distribution
- Water or particle ingress through worn seals
- Electrical pitting from stray shaft currents (common in VFD-driven motors)
- Fatigue — exceeding L10 design life
- Improper installation: press-fit damage, incorrect preload

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Vibration frequency analysis: peaks at bearing defect frequencies indicate specific race or rolling element damage
- Grease discolouration (black/brown) indicates contamination or overheating
- High-frequency vibration (>1 kHz) is the earliest indicator of bearing degradation
- Onset of noise during cold start that diminishes as machine warms indicates lubrication issue

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Stop machine if vibration >14 mm/s or temperature >95°C — risk of catastrophic failure
2. Take oil/grease sample for particle analysis
3. Perform vibration spectrum analysis to confirm bearing defect frequencies
4. Replace bearing and inspect shaft for scoring or corrosion
5. Check and replace seals to prevent re-contamination
6. Re-lubricate with correct lubricant type and quantity
7. Verify shaft alignment after bearing replacement
8. Check for shaft current if motor is inverter-driven — fit insulated bearing or shaft grounding ring

SEVERITY: HIGH — bearing failure is a leading cause of unplanned downtime
URGENCY: immediate if vibration >14 mm/s or temperature >90°C; otherwise schedule within 1–2 weeks

title: Engine and Motor Overheating
content:
FAULT: Engine and Motor Overheating
COMPONENT: Induction motors, reciprocating engines, compressors

SYMPTOMS:
- Elevated operating temperature (>80°C for motors, >95°C for compressors)
- Thermal protection relay tripping repeatedly
- Reduced output performance — loss of torque or speed
- Burning smell from windings or insulation
- Discolouration of motor casing
- Pressure drop in cooling circuits

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Temperature (°C): >75°C warn, >90°C danger — motor winding or casing
- Current (A): high current draw causes I²R heating — check against nameplate FLA
- Pressure (bar): if water-cooled, low coolant pressure indicates cooling failure
- Vibration (mm/s): may increase if thermal expansion causes mechanical distortion
- RPM: reduced speed under load if motor is near thermal limit

ROOT CAUSES:
- Blocked or clogged cooling fins/ventilation ducts — most common cause
- High ambient temperature exceeding motor's rated service factor
- Overloading — sustained current above full load amperes (FLA)
- Single-phase operation in three-phase motor (one phase lost)
- Excessive start/stop cycling without adequate cooling time
- Winding insulation deterioration — increased resistance, more heat
- Cooling fan failure or reversed rotation

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Compare actual current to nameplate FLA — overloading if ratio >1.0
- Check cooling fan rotation direction and air flow through motor
- Measure winding resistance (should be balanced ±10% across phases)
- Inspect air inlet screens for dust and debris blockage
- Thermal imaging shows hot spots in windings if insulation is failing

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Allow machine to cool before inspection — risk of burns
2. Clean all cooling fins, air inlet screens, and ventilation ducts
3. Verify cooling fan is functional and rotating in correct direction
4. Check power supply — confirm all three phases are present and balanced
5. Measure and compare operating current to nameplate rating
6. Test winding insulation resistance with megger (>1 MΩ minimum)
7. Verify ambient temperature is within motor's rated range
8. Check overload relay setting matches motor nameplate FLA

SEVERITY: HIGH — sustained overheating degrades winding insulation, leading to winding failure
URGENCY: immediate if temperature >95°C or thermal protection trips; soon otherwise

title: Lubrication System Failure and Oil Degradation
content:
FAULT: Lubrication Failure and Oil Degradation
COMPONENT: Gearboxes, bearings, engines, compressors, hydraulic systems

SYMPTOMS:
- Rapid temperature rise in gearbox or bearing housing (>85°C)
- Increased vibration and metallic noise from friction surfaces
- Oil pressure below normal operating range
- Metal particle contamination in oil sample
- Discoloured or burnt-smelling oil (black/brown vs amber)
- High wear rates — elevated iron/copper in spectrometric oil analysis

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Temperature (°C): >80°C warn, >95°C danger at gearbox or bearing housing
- Pressure (bar): low oil pressure <2 bar indicates pump failure or blocked filter
- Vibration (mm/s): rising vibration as lubrication film breaks down
- Noise (dB): metallic grinding or screeching as metal-to-metal contact increases
- Current (A): increasing current draw as friction load rises

ROOT CAUSES:
- Oil level too low — leak from seals, gaskets, or drain plug
- Lubricant viscosity incorrect — too thin (thermal breakdown) or too thick (inadequate flow)
- Oil filter blocked — restricts flow to critical surfaces
- Oil pump worn or failed — loss of pressure
- Water contamination in oil — oil appears milky or cloudy
- Lubricant oxidation from excessive heat — oil turns black and acidic
- Wrong lubricant specified — mixing incompatible oils

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Check oil level sight glass or dipstick — obvious first step
- Oil sample analysis (ferrography) will show elevated wear metals if problem is active
- Milky oil appearance indicates water contamination — check for coolant leaks
- Burnt smell and black colour indicate thermal breakdown of base oil
- Oil filter pressure differential >0.5 bar above clean baseline indicates blockage

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Top up oil level immediately if low — do not run dry
2. Send oil sample for laboratory analysis (viscosity, TAN, wear metals)
3. Replace oil filter — always replace when changing oil
4. Flush system and replace oil if contamination is confirmed
5. Identify and repair source of oil loss (seals, gaskets, fittings)
6. Verify correct oil specification as per OEM recommendation
7. Inspect and replace oil pump if pressure cannot be maintained
8. Set up regular oil analysis schedule every 500–1000 operating hours

SEVERITY: HIGH — lubrication failure causes accelerated wear and seizure
URGENCY: immediate if oil pressure <1.5 bar or temperature >95°C

title: Shaft Misalignment
content:
FAULT: Shaft Misalignment
COMPONENT: Shaft couplings, motor-to-pump/fan/compressor drive trains

SYMPTOMS:
- High vibration at 1× and 2× running speed (angular misalignment generates 2× dominant peak)
- Elevated coupling and bearing temperatures
- Excessive current draw from motor
- Rapid coupling wear or failure — coupling elements cracking or deforming
- Vibration increases immediately after maintenance or re-assembly
- Uneven wear on coupling spiders or flexible elements

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): >7.1 warn, >11.0 danger — typically dominant in axial direction for angular misalignment, radial for parallel
- Temperature (°C): coupling housing >65°C indicates excessive flexing/friction
- Current (A): elevated current >10% above baseline — shaft torque fluctuating
- Noise (dB): rhythmic thumping or knocking at shaft rotation frequency
- RPM: generally stable unless severe — compare drive end vs non-drive end vibration

ROOT CAUSES:
- Incorrect alignment during installation or after maintenance
- Thermal growth — machine moves when it reaches operating temperature
- Pipe strain — connected pipework putting force on pump casing
- Soft foot — machine baseplate not sitting flat, twisting frame
- Foundation settling or grouting degradation
- Worn coupling elements allowing angular play to develop

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Vibration spectrum: 2× running speed dominates for angular, 1× for parallel misalignment
- Phase measurement: 180° phase difference across coupling confirms misalignment
- Coupling element inspection: uneven wear pattern indicates direction of misalignment
- Laser alignment check quantifies offset and angularity
- Check soft foot before any alignment work — correct this first

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Perform soft foot check — correct before attempting alignment
2. Allow machine to reach operating temperature, then check alignment hot if possible
3. Perform precision laser shaft alignment — target <0.05 mm offset, <0.05 mm/100mm angularity
4. Check and relieve pipe strain — add flexible connections if required
5. Inspect and replace worn coupling elements
6. Check foundation integrity — look for cracked grouting
7. Verify alignment after first run at operating temperature
8. Document alignment readings for baseline comparison

SEVERITY: MEDIUM-HIGH — unresolved misalignment rapidly destroys couplings and bearings
URGENCY: soon — schedule alignment at next maintenance window unless vibration is severe

title: Pump Cavitation
content:
FAULT: Pump Cavitation
COMPONENT: Centrifugal pumps, mixed-flow pumps, axial pumps

SYMPTOMS:
- Crackling, rattling, or gravel-like noise from pump casing (sound of imploding bubbles)
- Erratic flow rate and pressure — fluctuating delivery
- Loss of pump head — flow rate drops below design point
- Elevated vibration at blade pass frequency and random broadband noise
- Pitting and erosion damage on impeller vanes and casing (visible on inspection)
- High noise level (>85 dB) at pump casing

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Pressure (bar): suction pressure low — NPSH available <NPSH required
- Vibration (mm/s): >5 mm/s with broadband random component
- Noise (dB): >85 dB, characteristic crackling distinct from normal pump noise
- Flow: reduced and unstable — pump operating left of design point on curve
- Temperature (°C): may rise slightly due to energy dissipation in vapour bubbles
- Current (A): may fluctuate as torque varies with unstable flow

ROOT CAUSES:
- Insufficient NPSH available — suction head too low
- Suction pipe restriction — blocked strainer, partially closed valve, undersized pipe
- Pump operating far from best efficiency point (BEP) — off-design operation
- High fluid temperature — vapour pressure elevated, reducing NPSH margin
- Air leaking into suction line — worn shaft seal or loose joint
- Pump speed too high for installed suction conditions
- Recirculation cavitation — pump operating at very low flow (<30% BEP)

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Check suction pressure gauge — reading lower than design NPSH available
- Noise is characteristic: crackling/rattling is cavitation; high-pitched whine is recirculation
- Reduced flow with unchanged speed strongly indicates cavitation
- Inspect impeller for pitting damage if symptom has persisted
- Raise suction tank level or lower pump elevation temporarily to test — if symptoms reduce, cavitation confirmed

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Check and clean suction strainer/filter — most common quick fix
2. Fully open suction isolation valve — verify it is not partially closed
3. Check suction pipe for blockage, kinks, or undersized sections
4. Reduce pump speed if VFD-equipped — operate closer to BEP
5. Check fluid temperature — reduce if possible to lower vapour pressure
6. Inspect and replace shaft seal if air ingress is suspected
7. Increase suction tank level if available
8. Inspect impeller for erosion damage and replace if required

SEVERITY: HIGH — impeller erosion damage accumulates rapidly once cavitation begins
URGENCY: soon — address within days to prevent impeller damage; immediate if vibration >10 mm/s

title: Belt Drive Failure and Wear
content:
FAULT: Belt Drive Failure and Wear
COMPONENT: V-belt and flat belt drives on fans, compressors, pumps

SYMPTOMS:
- Squealing or chirping noise — classic belt slip sound, especially on startup
- High vibration at belt pass frequency (belt length / drive speed)
- Reduced driven machine speed — slipping belt reducing power transmission
- Belt debris (rubber dust, cracked pieces) visible around drive
- Misaligned pulleys cause belt to ride on one edge — uneven wear
- Belt temperature elevated — can be felt or seen with thermal camera

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): elevated at belt pass frequency — typically 3–8× running speed sidebands
- RPM: driven shaft speed lower than expected if belt is slipping
- Noise (dB): intermittent squeal peaking >85 dB
- Temperature: belt surface >60°C indicates slipping or overloading
- Current (A): motor current may be high if belt is tight and overloaded

ROOT CAUSES:
- Belt elongation from wear — correct tension cannot be maintained
- Belt tension too low on installation — stretching and slipping
- Pulley misalignment — belt running at angle causes edge wear
- Belt contamination with oil or water — reduces friction coefficient
- Overloading — transmitted power exceeds belt drive capacity
- UV degradation and environmental cracking of rubber compound
- Using matched belt sets but mixing different manufacturers or ages

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Deflection test: belt should deflect 15–20 mm per 1 m span under moderate thumb pressure
- Pulley groove wear — check for polished or concave groove profile
- Belt cross-section profile — worn belt shows trapezoidal profile becoming rectangular
- Pulley alignment check: straightedge across pulley faces should show no gap

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Inspect belt condition — replace if cracked, glazed, or worn past minimum thickness
2. Check and correct belt tension using tension gauge or deflection method
3. Align pulleys using laser or straightedge — maximum 0.5 mm misalignment
4. Clean pulley grooves of oil and debris — use brake cleaner
5. Replace pulleys if grooves are worn (concave profile)
6. Replace all belts as a matched set — do not mix old and new
7. Check that drive is correctly sized for transmitted load
8. Re-tension new belts after 4–8 hours of initial run

SEVERITY: MEDIUM — belt failure causes loss of driven machine function
URGENCY: scheduled — replace at next opportunity; immediate if squeal is continuous or belt is cracked

title: Mechanical Rotor Imbalance
content:
FAULT: Mechanical Rotor Imbalance
COMPONENT: Fans, blowers, impellers, rotors, compressor wheels

SYMPTOMS:
- Strong vibration at exactly 1× running speed (fundamental frequency) — dominant peak in spectrum
- Vibration is strongly directional — typically largest in radial (horizontal/vertical) planes
- Vibration amplitude proportional to speed squared (increases with RPM)
- Stable, consistent vibration — does not vary randomly like bearing noise
- Possible visible wobble or oscillation of shaft or machine casing
- Premature bearing wear from sustained unbalanced centrifugal force

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): >7.1 warn, >11.0 danger — clean 1× peak in spectrum
- RPM: stable — vibration tracks speed changes proportionally
- Noise (dB): rhythmic at rotation frequency, not random
- Temperature (°C): may rise at bearings from increased load
- Current (A): slight increase from additional centrifugal loading on motor

ROOT CAUSES:
- Material build-up on rotor (dust, scale, product, ice) — common in fans
- Loss of balance weight — weight flew off during operation
- Blade erosion or damage — asymmetric material loss
- Uneven fouling or corrosion on impeller vanes
- Residual imbalance from manufacture — not corrected during factory balancing
- Component replacement without re-balancing the rotor
- Shaft bow — bent shaft creates dynamic imbalance

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Spectrum: single clean peak at 1× RPM — this is the imbalance signature
- Phase measurement: consistent phase angle that rotates with the shaft
- Compare horizontal and vertical vibration — if equal and 90° out of phase: pure imbalance
- Inspect rotor for material deposits or missing balance weights
- Run at different speeds — vibration amplitude scales with N² (speed squared)

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Inspect rotor for material build-up — clean fan blades and impeller thoroughly
2. Inspect for missing, damaged, or loose balance weights
3. Check for blade damage or asymmetric erosion — repair or replace blades
4. Perform in-situ dynamic balancing using vibration analyser and trial weights
5. If balancing cannot correct imbalance: remove rotor and perform workshop balancing
6. Check shaft for bend — runout >0.05 mm indicates bent shaft, requires replacement
7. After balancing, verify vibration <2.5 mm/s RMS for fans, <1.8 mm/s for precision machines

SEVERITY: MEDIUM — imbalance accelerates bearing wear but rarely causes immediate failure
URGENCY: scheduled — balance within 2–4 weeks; immediate if vibration >14 mm/s

title: Motor Electrical Fault — Winding and Supply Issues
content:
FAULT: Motor Electrical Fault
COMPONENT: Induction motors — stator windings, rotor bars, supply conductors

SYMPTOMS:
- Excessive current draw — motor running above nameplate full load amps (FLA)
- Motor tripping on overload or overcurrent protection repeatedly
- Elevated motor temperature from I²R losses
- Vibration at twice supply frequency (100 Hz) indicates electrical origin
- Unbalanced phase currents (>10% variation between phases)
- Burning smell from windings — insulation breakdown

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Current (A): >nameplate FLA warn; >120% FLA danger; >150% FLA immediate trip
- Temperature (°C): >80°C warn, >100°C danger — motor winding temperature
- Vibration (mm/s): elevated with 2× supply frequency (100 Hz) electrical vibration
- Noise (dB): electrical hum louder than normal — magnetic noise
- RPM: reduced under load if rotor bars are broken (slip increases)

ROOT CAUSES:
- Phase loss or voltage imbalance — one phase fuse blown or connection loose
- Voltage too low — motor draws higher current to maintain torque
- Voltage too high — increased core losses, overheating
- Winding insulation failure — short circuit between turns, phase-to-phase, or phase-to-earth
- Broken rotor bars — causes asymmetric torque, increased slip, and current draw
- Mechanical overload — driven machine seized or jammed, motor fights against it
- Single-phasing on three-phase motor — causes current in remaining phases to reach 173% of normal

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Current clamp measurement on all three phases — compare to nameplate and to each other
- Voltage measurement at motor terminals — should be within ±5% of rated, and balanced
- Winding resistance measurement (balanced within ±5% per phase)
- Insulation resistance (megger test): >1 MΩ phase-to-earth; <100 kΩ indicates failure
- Motor current signature analysis (MCSA): detects broken rotor bars via slip frequency sidebands
- Disconnect motor from load — if current normalises, fault is mechanical overload

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Check supply voltage at motor terminals — record all three phases
2. Measure and compare current in all three phases — identify imbalance
3. Megger test winding insulation — record phase-to-phase and phase-to-earth
4. Measure winding resistance with milliohm meter — check for open turns
5. Check and tighten all terminal connections in motor junction box
6. Verify driven machine turns freely by hand — rule out mechanical seizure
7. If winding fault confirmed: rewind or replace motor
8. Fit voltage monitoring relay to detect future phase loss events

SEVERITY: HIGH — winding failure is expensive and causes extended downtime
URGENCY: immediate if current >150% FLA or insulation resistance <100 kΩ

title: Excessive Mechanical Vibration — General
content:
FAULT: Excessive Mechanical Vibration
COMPONENT: Any rotating or reciprocating machine

SYMPTOMS:
- Vibration velocity >7.1 mm/s RMS (ISO 10816 Zone C — requires correction)
- Vibration >11.0 mm/s RMS (ISO 10816 Zone D — immediate shutdown recommended)
- Audible increase in noise level
- Loosening of fasteners (bolts working loose repeatedly)
- Accelerated wear on seals, couplings, and bearings
- Fatigue cracks appearing in welds, supports, or machine casing

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): severity classification per ISO 10816:
  * Class I small machines: Zone A <0.71, B <1.8, C <4.5, D >4.5
  * Class II medium machines (15–75 kW): Zone A <1.12, B <2.8, C <7.1, D >7.1
  * Class III large machines: Zone A <1.8, B <4.5, C <11.2, D >11.2
- Frequency of vibration identifies root cause:
  * 1× RPM: imbalance, misalignment (parallel), bent shaft
  * 2× RPM: angular misalignment, looseness
  * 0.5× RPM: oil whirl in journal bearings
  * Non-synchronous: bearing defect frequencies, gear mesh, belt frequency

ROOT CAUSES (listed by vibration frequency signature):
- 1× RPM dominant: mechanical imbalance, shaft bow, resonance at running speed
- 2× RPM dominant: angular misalignment, looseness, cracked shaft
- Multiple harmonics: mechanical looseness, foundation problems, gear wear
- Broadband random: bearing damage, cavitation, turbulence, fluid-induced vibration
- Sub-synchronous: oil whirl (<0.5×), stall in fans/compressors
- Electrical frequencies (100 Hz, 50 Hz sidebands): motor electrical faults, rotor bar defects

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Vibration spectrum analysis is essential — time waveform and FFT spectrum together
- Phase measurement across coupling identifies misalignment vs imbalance
- Check structural resonance — operate at different speeds to confirm resonance amplification
- Compare drive end vs non-drive end — localises the source
- Check foundation bolts for looseness — hand tight vs properly torqued difference is detectable

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Record baseline spectrum before making any changes
2. Check for and correct mechanical looseness (bolts, mounts, hold-down bolts)
3. Perform shaft alignment check — correct to within tolerance
4. Inspect and clean rotor for build-up or imbalance
5. Inspect bearings — replace if defect frequencies are present in spectrum
6. Check foundation integrity — repair cracked or degraded grouting
7. If resonance suspected — detune by adding mass, stiffening structure, or changing speed

SEVERITY: VARIABLE — depends on vibration level and rate of change
URGENCY: immediate if >11 mm/s; soon if 7–11 mm/s; scheduled if 4–7 mm/s

title: Cooling System Failure
content:
FAULT: Cooling System Failure
COMPONENT: Cooling fans, heat exchangers, water-cooling circuits, radiators

SYMPTOMS:
- Machine temperature rising above normal operating range
- Coolant flow rate reduced or zero
- Coolant pressure drop across heat exchanger
- Cooling fan not running or running slowly
- High ambient temperature inside enclosure
- Automatic shutdown on high temperature protection

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Temperature (°C): rising above design operating point — check against OEM limits
- Pressure (bar): low coolant pressure <2 bar in water-cooled systems
- Current (A): cooling fan motor current — zero if fan has failed
- Flow rate: if measured, below minimum design flow indicates pump or blockage issue

ROOT CAUSES:
- Cooling fan motor failure — bearing failure, winding fault, capacitor failure
- Blocked heat exchanger tubes — scale, fouling, or biological growth
- Coolant pump failure — impeller wear, seal failure, cavitation
- Low coolant level — leak from pipes, fittings, or heat exchanger
- Thermostat stuck closed — coolant not circulating to radiator
- Air lock in cooling circuit — prevents coolant circulation
- Fouled air side of radiator or cooler — dust/debris blocking airflow

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Check cooling fan rotation — confirm it is running and in correct direction
- Feel inlet and outlet coolant pipes — outlet should be hot, inlet warm (if thermostat open)
- Inspect air-side of cooler for blockage — can clean with compressed air
- Pressure test cooling system to identify leaks
- Check coolant level in expansion tank — low level indicates leak

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Check cooling fan operation — confirm running and correct direction
2. Clean air-side of heat exchanger with compressed air or water jet
3. Check coolant level and top up if low — investigate leak source
4. Flush cooling system if scale or fouling is suspected
5. Test coolant pump — verify flow rate and pressure output
6. Inspect thermostat — replace if stuck
7. Bleed air from cooling system if air lock is suspected
8. Replace heat exchanger if tube fouling cannot be cleared

SEVERITY: HIGH — cooling failure rapidly leads to thermal damage
URGENCY: immediate if temperature is approaching trip setpoint and rising

title: Low Oil Pressure
content:
FAULT: Low Oil Pressure
COMPONENT: Engines, gearboxes, hydraulic systems, lubrication circuits

SYMPTOMS:
- Oil pressure gauge reading below normal operating range
- Low oil pressure alarm or shutdown activation
- Elevated bearing and journal temperatures from reduced lubrication film
- Increased noise — metallic knocking if hydrodynamic film collapses
- Increased vibration from lack of oil film damping in journal bearings

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Pressure (bar): oil pressure <2.0 bar warn, <1.5 bar danger (typical; verify OEM spec)
- Temperature (°C): bearing temperature rising rapidly when oil pressure is lost
- Vibration (mm/s): increasing as oil film breaks down
- Noise (dB): metallic knock or rumble if metal-to-metal contact begins
- Flow: oil flow meter reading low if pump output has dropped

ROOT CAUSES:
- Oil level too low — most common and easiest to correct
- Oil pump wear — gear pump teeth worn, reduced volumetric efficiency
- Oil filter clogged — pressure drop through filter reduces delivery pressure
- Pressure relief valve stuck open — bypasses oil before it reaches bearings
- Oil viscosity too low — hot oil or wrong grade reduces film pressure
- Internal oil leak — cracked passage, blown gasket, worn seal diverting flow
- Oil cooler blockage — oil overheats, viscosity drops, pressure cannot be maintained

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Check oil level first — simple and most common cause
- Check oil filter — replace if over age or pressure differential is high
- Measure oil viscosity if available — compare to specification
- Inspect pressure relief valve — temporarily plug if stuck open to test
- Pressure test lubrication circuit to identify internal leak location

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Check and top up oil level immediately — do not run with low oil pressure
2. Replace oil filter — always change filter when investigating low pressure
3. Inspect pressure relief valve — clean and test, replace if faulty
4. Send oil sample for viscosity test — replace oil if degraded
5. Test oil pump output pressure and flow — replace pump if below specification
6. Inspect all oil passages and gaskets for internal leaks
7. Check oil cooler for blockage — clean if fouled
8. Fit permanent oil pressure monitoring with auto-shutdown if not already installed

SEVERITY: CRITICAL — operating without adequate oil pressure causes rapid bearing and journal damage
URGENCY: immediate — stop machine if pressure is below minimum and cannot be restored

title: Mechanical Seal and Shaft Seal Failure
content:
FAULT: Mechanical Seal and Shaft Seal Failure
COMPONENT: Pump shaft seals, compressor seals, gearbox lip seals

SYMPTOMS:
- Visible fluid leakage around shaft area
- Reduced system pressure or flow due to internal bypass
- Oil level dropping without external leaks visible
- High noise from air ingestion on pump suction side (cavitation-like)
- Bearing contamination from leaked fluid entering bearing housing
- Increased vibration if seal is dragging on shaft

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Pressure (bar): reduced suction or discharge pressure if seal leaks on pump
- Vibration (mm/s): slight increase if seal is rubbing or causing shaft deflection
- Temperature (°C): seal area may be hot if running dry (seal faces contacting without fluid)
- Noise (dB): hissing if pressurised gas leaking; sucking sound if air ingress on suction side
- Current (A): may decrease if pump is cavitating due to air ingress from failed seal

ROOT CAUSES:
- Seal faces worn or scored — normal wear beyond service life
- Dry running — seal faces running without flush fluid (flushes evaporated or not connected)
- Misalignment — shaft deflection causes seal face to tilt and leak
- Vibration — excessive vibration causes dynamic seal to hammer on faces
- Chemical attack — process fluid incompatible with seal face material
- Improper installation — faces not flat, wrong spring compression, damaged O-rings
- Cavitation — pressure fluctuations cause seal face flutter and rapid wear

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Inspect seal area visually — identify leak location and fluid type
- Check seal flush line is flowing and at correct pressure (typically 1.5–3 bar above stuffing box pressure)
- Check shaft runout at seal — >0.05 mm TIR indicates misalignment or shaft deflection
- Examine failed seal faces — scoring or heat discolouration indicates dry running

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Document leak rate and fluid type — assess urgency of shutdown
2. Confirm seal flush is operational and at correct pressure
3. Check shaft alignment — correct before fitting new seal
4. Replace mechanical seal with correct spare — use manufacturer's installation procedure
5. Inspect shaft sleeve for scoring — replace if score marks exceed 0.1 mm depth
6. Verify correct seal type for process fluid and temperature
7. Flush new seal faces with clean fluid before startup
8. Monitor for repeat failure — investigate root cause if seal fails again within 6 months

SEVERITY: MEDIUM — leakage is hazardous and causes environmental and safety issues
URGENCY: soon for minor weeping; immediate for spray leaks or flammable/toxic fluids

title: Gearbox Overheating
content:
FAULT: Gearbox Overheating
COMPONENT: Industrial gearboxes — helical, bevel, worm, planetary

SYMPTOMS:
- Gearbox oil temperature >80°C (oil sump temperature)
- Elevated gear tooth and bearing temperatures
- Burnt or degraded oil smell
- Increased vibration from thermal distortion of gear mesh geometry
- Gear tooth wear marks or scoring visible on inspection
- Oil pressure dropping as oil viscosity falls with temperature

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Temperature (°C): oil sump >80°C warn, >100°C danger
- Vibration (mm/s): gear mesh frequency vibration increasing as thermal distortion grows
- Pressure (bar): oil pressure drops as oil thins with high temperature
- Noise (dB): gear whine intensity increases with poor lubrication
- Current (A): rising current if gear friction is increasing load on motor

ROOT CAUSES:
- Insufficient lubrication — oil level low or pump failure
- Wrong oil viscosity grade — too low a viscosity for operating temperature
- Overloading — gearbox running above rated torque capacity continuously
- Cooling fan failed or blocked — air-cooled gearbox losing cooling
- Oil cooler fouled — water-cooled gearbox not rejecting heat
- Excessive gear tooth wear — poor meshing, increased friction and heat generation
- Worm gearbox in high duty cycle — inherently inefficient, generates heat

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Check oil level and condition — first step for any thermal issue
- Oil sample: elevated viscosity drop or high wear metal content indicates active degradation
- Compare actual gearbox power loss to design efficiency — excess heat = efficiency loss
- Thermal imaging: identifies hot spots on casing indicating gear or bearing locations
- Gear inspection: scoring, pitting, or micropitting on tooth flanks

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Check oil level and top up immediately if low
2. Send oil sample for viscosity and contamination analysis
3. Drain and replace oil if degraded — black, burnt-smelling, or water contaminated
4. Clean cooling fins or cooler — restore full heat rejection capacity
5. Verify gearbox is operating within rated load limits
6. Check and replace gear oil to correct viscosity grade per OEM specification
7. Inspect gear teeth on next available shutdown — look for scoring or pitting
8. Fit oil temperature monitoring with high-temperature alarm if not installed

SEVERITY: HIGH — unchecked overheating causes catastrophic gear tooth or bearing failure
URGENCY: immediate if temperature >100°C or oil pressure low; soon if temperature rising trend

title: Coupling Failure and Wear
content:
FAULT: Coupling Failure and Wear
COMPONENT: Flexible couplings, jaw couplings, disc couplings, gear couplings

SYMPTOMS:
- Vibration increase at 1× and 2× running speed
- Irregular knocking or banging at shaft rotation frequency
- Coupling element (spider, disc pack, elastomer) cracking or fragmenting
- Elevated temperature at coupling housing
- Shaft misalignment worsening over time as coupling wears
- Complete loss of power transmission if coupling fails catastrophically

SENSOR INDICATORS:
- Vibration (mm/s): increasing at 1× and 2× running speed; sudden step change indicates coupling failure
- Temperature (°C): coupling housing temperature >60°C indicates excessive flexing
- Noise (dB): knocking or thumping at running frequency
- Current (A): fluctuating or elevated if coupling is slipping or transmitting torque irregularly
- RPM: driven shaft speed drops or becomes unstable if coupling is slipping

ROOT CAUSES:
- Shaft misalignment — most common cause of coupling wear; flexible elements absorbing misalignment degrade
- Operating above coupling rated torque — overloading coupling capacity
- Angular misalignment beyond coupling rated capacity
- Chemical attack on elastomer elements — oil, solvents, or process fluids
- Incorrect coupling selection — wrong type or size for the application
- Age and fatigue — elastomers harden and crack, metals fatigue
- High cyclic loading — frequent starts and stops, or reversing applications

DIAGNOSTIC CLUES:
- Inspect coupling spider or disc pack: cracks, chunking, or compression set visible
- Check coupling alignment — if coupling is wearing, there is almost always misalignment
- Measure coupling temperature with contact probe or thermal camera
- Vibration phase measurement across coupling: 180° phase shift confirms misalignment causing coupling stress

MAINTENANCE ACTIONS:
1. Inspect coupling element condition — replace if cracked, deformed, or worn
2. Check shaft alignment before replacing coupling — do not replace without correcting misalignment
3. Perform precision laser shaft alignment — bring within tolerance
4. Verify correct coupling type and torque rating for application
5. Check for torsional vibration if coupling failures are recurring — may need torsionally softer coupling
6. Inspect coupling hubs for fretting or spline wear — replace hubs if damaged
7. Document coupling failure mode for root cause tracking

SEVERITY: MEDIUM-HIGH — failed coupling causes loss of drive; failure can also damage connected machinery
URGENCY: immediate if coupling is fragmenting; soon if cracks are found on inspection
